title: Tharu Culture in Chitwan: Villages, Food and History
meta_description: Tharu culture in Chitwan: who the Tharu are, their mud-walled villages, food such as dhikri and ghonghi, the Maghi festival and how to visit respectfully.
summary: The Tharu are the original people of Chitwan and the wider Terai, living in these forests long before the national park. Visit a village near Sauraha, stay in a community homestay in Barauli or Amaltari, eat dhikri and river snails, and time your trip for Maghi in January to see Tharu culture at its most joyful.

sections.heading: Who the Tharu are
paras: The Tharu are one of Nepal's largest indigenous peoples, about six percent of the population, living along almost the whole length of the Terai from Jhapa in the east to Kanchanpur in the west, and across the border in India. They speak several related Tharu languages, have their own gods, festivals and clan systems, and for centuries farmed, fished and hunted in the forested plains that most hill people avoided because of malaria.

There is no single Tharu culture. Communities differ from east to west in dress, house style, dialect and ritual. The Tharu of Chitwan and Nawalpur are often called Chitwania Tharu; those of Dang, Banke and Bardia, Dangaura Tharu; and those of Kailali and Kanchanpur, Rana Tharu. In Chitwan you will meet Tharu families running homestays, guiding in the park, farming rice and mustard, and keeping traditions alive through dance groups, cooking and festivals.

sections.heading: Life before the park and the highway
paras: Until the 1950s, the Chitwan valley was thick forest and grassland, home mainly to Tharu, Bote, Darai and Kumal communities, and feared by outsiders for its malaria. The Rana rulers kept it as a royal hunting reserve. The most famous hunt came in 1911, when King George V of Britain shot dozens of tigers and rhino here in a few weeks, a scale of killing that now feels hard to imagine.

Everything changed in the mid-1950s, when a malaria control programme using DDT made the valley safe for settlers. The government resettled thousands of families from the hills, forests were cleared for farms, and many Tharu lost land they had farmed for generations but did not hold on paper. When the national park was created in 1973, more villages were moved out of the core area. Studies have suggested that many Tharu carry some inherited resistance to malaria, which may help explain how they thrived where others could not.

Further west, many Tharu families fell into bonded labour under the kamaiya system, working for landlords to pay off debts. Nepal abolished kamaiya labour in 2000, and the related kamlari system, under which young Tharu girls were sent to work as domestic servants, was formally ended by the government in 2013. These histories still shape Tharu politics and pride today.

sections.heading: Tharu villages and houses
paras: A traditional Tharu house is built from a frame of timber and reeds, plastered with a mix of mud and cow dung, and roofed with thatch or, more often now, tiles or tin. Walls are smooth and cool, often decorated with relief patterns of animals, birds and plants, and in some homes painted in red and white. Inside, grain is stored in large clay bins, and the kitchen and family shrine are kept clean and private.

Around the house you will see fish traps woven from bamboo, ducks and pigs, buffalo and goats, and stacks of firewood and thatch. Many villages near Sauraha now mix old and new houses, concrete next to mud and reed. Walking through them with a local guide, early in the morning or late afternoon, is one of the best ways to understand how people here live beside the park.

sections.heading: Food: dhikri, ghonghi and rice beer
paras: Tharu food is built on rice, fish and whatever the river and forest provide. The dish most visitors try is dhikri: rice-flour dough shaped by hand into long, twisted or round pieces and steamed, eaten with chutney, curry or vegetables. It is made for festivals and special guests, and homestay hosts are happy to teach you.

Ghonghi, freshwater snails collected from paddy fields and ponds, are another favourite, cooked in a spicy gravy and eaten by sucking the meat from the shell. You may also be served river fish, freshwater crab, duck, wild greens and a mild home-brewed rice beer. Meals in a homestay are simple and generous, eaten on the floor or at a low table.
list: Dhikri: steamed rice-flour dumplings, the classic Tharu dish
Ghonghi: river snails in spicy gravy, seasonal
Fish and crab: from the rivers and ponds, curried or fried
Rice beer: brewed at home, mild and slightly sour

sections.heading: Festivals and dance
paras: The most important Tharu festival is Maghi, which falls on the first day of the month of Magh, around mid-January, the same day as Maghe Sankranti for other Nepalis. For the Tharu it is the start of the new year, a time for family reunions, feasts with plenty of dhikri, pork and rice beer, ritual bathing and days of dancing. Maghe Sankranti is a public holiday, and Tharu towns and villages shut down for the celebrations.

The stick dance, performed by young men and boys who strike sticks together in fast, intricate patterns, is the dance most visitors see in Sauraha's cultural shows. It is said to have begun as a way of scaring off wild animals, and it is still danced at village festivals. Women's dances, with songs and swaying lines, are performed at weddings and festivals too.

sections.heading: Where to experience Tharu culture
paras: You do not need to go far from Chitwan's lodges to meet Tharu culture, but how you do it matters. A walk with a local guide or a night in a community homestay gives a far better picture than a staged show alone.

sections.heading: A day in a Tharu homestay
paras: A homestay day starts early. Before sunrise the courtyard is swept, the buffalo are milked and someone is already feeding the fire for tea, often sweet and milky. Guests are welcome to join in or to sleep on; nobody minds. After breakfast you might walk to the fields with your hosts, help with whatever the season demands, from planting rice in July to cutting mustard in February, or go with the women to collect fodder at the edge of the community forest.

The middle of the day is slow, and the afternoon is the time to cook. Shaping dhikri by hand takes practice, and the family will laugh kindly at your first attempts. In the evening neighbours drop by, children practise their English, and a youth group may perform a dance in the village yard. Dinner is rice, lentils, vegetables and perhaps fish or duck, eaten late by Nepali standards and early by yours. Lights go out soon after, and the night belongs to frogs, crickets and, sometimes, a rhino wandering through the fields.

sections.heading: Visiting with respect
paras: Tharu villages are homes, not museums. Ask before photographing people, especially women and older people, and do not walk into houses, kitchens or shrines unless invited. Dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees. Shoes come off before entering most homes.

Buy crafts directly from makers when you can, and choose community homestays where income is shared fairly through a committee. If you watch a cultural show, the money usually supports a local youth or women's group. A few words of greeting go a long way, and most Tharu also speak Nepali. Above all, ask questions and listen: the best stories in Chitwan are told on a mud verandah over tea.

faqs.a: The Tharu are an indigenous people of Nepal's Terai and neighbouring parts of India, about six percent of Nepal's population. They have lived in the forests and plains of the Terai for centuries, farming, fishing and hunting, and speak several related Tharu languages. Communities differ from east to west, with distinct dress, houses and festivals.

faqs.q: What is the Tharu stick dance?
faqs.a: A fast, rhythmic dance in which young men strike wooden sticks together in changing patterns, often in a circle, to drums and song. It is said to have begun as a way of scaring off wild animals. In Sauraha it is performed most evenings for visitors, and it is also part of village festivals.

Dhikri is the best-known Tharu dish: dumplings of rice flour shaped by hand and steamed, served with chutney, curry or vegetables. It is cooked for festivals such as Maghi and for honoured guests. Many homestays and some restaurants in Sauraha serve it, and homestay hosts often let you help make it.

faqs.q: When is Maghi, the Tharu new year?
faqs.a: Maghi falls on the first day of the Nepali month of Magh, usually around 14 or 15 January, the same day as Maghe Sankranti. Tharu communities celebrate with feasts, family gatherings, ritual bathing and several days of dancing. Villages hold dances for several days. Ask us about joining village celebrations as a guest.

faqs.q: Can I stay with a Tharu family in Chitwan?
faqs.a: Yes. Community homestays in Barauli and Amaltari, on the western side of Chitwan, let you stay with Tharu families, eat home-cooked meals and join daily life. Rooms are simple and clean. The village committee sets prices and shares the income among families and a community fund.

faqs.q: Are Tharu cultural shows in Sauraha authentic?
faqs.a: They are real dances performed by local Tharu groups, though shortened and staged for visitors. The money usually supports the dance group or a community organisation. For a fuller picture, combine a show with a village walk with a Tharu guide or a night in a community homestay, where dance, food and daily life come together.

faqs.q: What happened to the Tharu when Chitwan was settled?
faqs.a: From the mid-1950s, malaria control opened Chitwan to settlers from the hills, and the government resettled thousands of families there. Forests were cleared, and many Tharu lost land they farmed but did not formally own. The creation of the national park in 1973 moved more villages. Today Tharu are a minority in the district they once dominated.

Kamaiya was a system of bonded agricultural labour, mainly in western Nepal, in which Tharu families worked for landlords to repay debts that often passed between generations. Nepal abolished it in 2000. The related kamlari practice, sending young girls to work as domestic servants, was formally ended in 2013. Both remain part of Tharu memory.

faqs.q: How should I behave in a Tharu village?
faqs.a: Dress modestly, greet people with namaste, ask before taking photos and do not enter houses, kitchens or shrines unless invited. Take shoes off when you go indoors. Avoid giving money or sweets to children; support a school or buy crafts instead. Go with a local guide, who can introduce you and translate.
